title: Coddled Eggs
subtitle: Eggs set in a jar with cream and herbs, a gentle, old-fashioned method
excerpt: Coddled eggs are cooked in individual covered pots set in gently simmering water, producing a texture between a soft-boiled and a baked egg, tender, barely set, and scented with cream and herbs.
sourceNotes: Coddling is a traditional English technique described by Mrs Beeton in 'Book of Household Management' (1861) and common in Victorian and Edwardian households. The method uses gentle indirect heat to set the egg more softly than boiling or poaching.

recipe.temperatureNote: Water is kept at a gentle simmer, well below boiling, throughout cooking

glossaryTerms.definition: To cook food gently in water kept just below simmering point, around 75 to 82 °C. The result is softer and more delicate than boiling.
A method of gentle, indirect cooking where a container of food sits in a pan of hot water. The water moderates the heat so the food never exceeds 100 °C.

content.text: Coddled eggs are among the quietest and most forgiving things you can cook for breakfast. The egg goes into a small buttered pot with a spoonful of cream and a pinch of herbs, the pot goes into a pan of gently simmering water, and in about 10 minutes you have something with a texture unlike any other egg preparation: tender, just-set, and faintly enriched by the cream. The method is one of the oldest in the British kitchen, described by the Victorian cookery writer Mrs Beeton in the 1860s as a restorative for the unwell. It still earns its place.
What you need

You will need 2 egg coddlers, small heatproof jars with lids (such as Kilner jars with 200 ml capacity), or heatproof ramekins covered tightly with foil. The coddler must have a lid or covering to trap the steam that helps set the top of the egg.
Butter the inside of each coddler. Add 1 tbsp of cream, crack in an egg, scatter over chives, season with salt and pepper, and cover firmly with the lid or foil.
Place the coddlers in a pan of barely trembling water that reaches halfway up their sides. Cover the pan with a lid.
Cook for 8 to 10 minutes. Lift out with a tea towel and serve in the coddler with buttered toast alongside.
Prepare the coddlers
Butter the inside of each coddler or jar generously with the
unsalted-butter
. Pour 1 tbsp of
double-cream
into each one. Crack an egg in on top, trying not to break the yolk. Scatter half the
chives
over each egg, then season with a little sea salt and a grind of black pepper. Screw the lids on firmly or cover tightly with a square of foil, pressing it around the rim.
Coddle in the water bath
Half-fill the saucepan with water and bring it to a gentle
coddle
, the water should barely tremble rather than actively simmering. This is a
bain-marie

arrangement: the coddlers sit in the hot water and cook from the gentle heat radiating through the glass or porcelain. Set the coddlers in the pan; the water should come about halfway up their sides. Cover the pan with a lid and cook for 8 to 10 minutes.

At 8 minutes the egg will be barely set, a trembling, custard-like consistency. At 10 minutes the white will be set and the yolk will be soft but not flowing. Check by tilting the coddler gently: the contents should move in one piece rather than slosh. If the white still looks translucent and liquid at the top, give it another minute.
Serve in the coddler

Lift the coddlers out of the water with a tea towel, they will be hot. Set them on small plates. Serve in the coddler itself: the tradition is to bring it to the table and eat the egg directly from the pot with a small spoon. Fingers of buttered white toast or thinly sliced sourdough are the natural accompaniment for scooping.
Variations

The classic version with cream and chives is only a starting point. Smoked salmon or a few flakes of smoked haddock in the base is excellent. Grated Parmesan stirred into the cream adds depth. A scraping of truffle paste is the hotel-restaurant version. Coddled eggs are accommodating to whatever you have and forgiving of experimentation.
Troubleshooter

Egg still liquid after 10 minutes: the water was not hot enough, or the coddlers were very cold to start with. Make sure the water is hot before the coddlers go in, and warm the coddlers with a splash of hot water first if they have been sitting in a cold kitchen.

White is rubbery and cream has curdled: the water was too hot. The water should barely tremble, a proper coddle is a very gentle process. Reduce the heat and try again; the results at lower temperatures are markedly better.
Where this dish lives

Egg coddlers are a piece of Victorian and Edwardian England, manufactured in porcelain by Royal Worcester from the 1890s onwards and given as gifts for generations. The method fell out of fashion as the full English fry took over the weekend breakfast, but coddled eggs have quietly made a return in restaurants and homes that prefer a gentler, more considered start to the day. The Victorian cookery writer Mrs Beeton recommended them for invalids and convalescents. They are, as it turns out, excellent for anyone.
